To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) the range of values in a context influences the judged value of a stimulus in that context; (b) the range effect can be accounted for by a rank-based theory that assumes that judgments are determined by the relative ranked position (i.e., rank) of a stimulus within its context; and (c) the range effect is an artefact of the relative memorability (distinctiveness) of items in a context.

1) range effects can be accounted for by rank-based decision by sampling models when the relative memorabilities of contextual items are taken into account; and 2) the relative memorability (or salience) of items can be accounted for in terms of a memory model.

(1) range effects in judgment are due to the relative memorability, and thus rank, of the items in the context, and (2) this is a consequence of the fact that the context is sampled when making a judgment.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of whether and how contextual influences on preferences are determined by the relative ranked position, the range, or both of a stimulus in the context of judgment and choice.
how context affects judgment and choice and with the cognitive processes that underpin this.
the cognitive processes underlying judgment and choice in contexts of available options, and with the role of context and memory in these processes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

a rank-based model, such as the decision by sampling approach (Stewart, Chater & Brown, 2006) can account for apparent effects of range position in judgments of stimuli in a context, when the relative memorabilities of the context items are taken into account.
, in general, range effects in the context of a rank-based theory of judgment and choice can arise from the interaction of the memory for stimuli in context with their relative rank positions.
the decision by sampling and range frequency theory are both useful models, but the former is more general and more accurate.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
range frequency effects are not a challenge for the decision by sampling framework.
the context-dependency of preferences is not due to a range effect per se, but is due to a range-frequency effect.
a purely rank- based model can explain apparent range effects when memory effects are considered.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the apparent context effects that are observed in the laboratory and real world can be accounted for by a model that is entirely rank-based, and that does not need to assume that the range position of the target item matters.
the context-dependence of judgments and choices is a function of the relative memorability (and not the relative ranked position) of the stimuli in the judgment or choice context.
the relative rank of a stimulus in the context of judgment is the only information used by a decision maker, and that apparent range effects are an artifact of differential memorability.
